patch.objective: Recognize appendicitis by right lower quadrant or periumbilical pain and report it, since perforation can lead to peritonitis and sepsis

sources.note: Relayed from the LPN/VN course's earlier cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read for this band: the practical nursing course is built toward this test plan.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case clinic-belly-pain-moved-right, not re-read for this band; its note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-PN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Coordinated Care includes care within the legal scope of practice; Physiological Adaptation includes recognizing and reporting a change in the client's condition.

sources.cite: StatPearls (StatPearls Publishing, NCBI Bookshelf): Appendicitis (Nursing), nurse editor Beth A. Kendall, last updated 2024-02-12
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case clinic-belly-pain-moved-right, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes of the statpearls.com copy (NCBI refuses automated fetches): 'Classically, appendicitis presents as an initial generalized or periumbilical abdominal pain' that localizes to the right lower quadrant, with decreased appetite, nausea or vomiting, and fever in about 40%; right lower quadrant pain on palpation of the left lower quadrant; symptoms 'progress from early appendicitis at 12 to 24 hours to perforation at greater than 48 hours', with rupture risk rising after 36 hours; nurses 'alert the health care provider to symptoms of peritonitis, as this could indicate a ruptured appendix', including a 'board-like abdomen' with rigidity and guarding, and to tachycardia or fever.

Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case clinic-belly-pain-moved-right, not re-read for this band; its note: Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
